Analogia Entis
ah-NAH-lo-gee-ah EN-tis
Latin metaphysical principle (Catholic theology; Reformed critique)
Latin analogia (proportion, correspondence) + entis (of being, genitive of ens, a being, entity); the principle that there is a proportionate likeness (analogia) between created being and divine Being, allowing the human mind to reason from creaturely existence upward to God's existence and attributes; formally developed by Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologica, 1265–1274) on the basis of Aristotle's doctrine of analogy, and declared by Karl Barth to be “the invention of antichrist” in his Church Dogmatics (1932)

Biblical Definition

The analogia entis — analogy of being — is the Catholic metaphysical principle that created being stands in a proportionate relationship to divine Being, and that the human mind can therefore reason from the existence and properties of creatures to a genuine (if imperfect) knowledge of God. The principle draws on Paul's statement in Romans 1:20 that “since the creation of the world His invisible attributes — His eternal power and divine nature — have been clearly seen, being understood through what has been made.” That much is common ground: the creation does reveal God. The Reformed tradition, however, distinguishes sharply between the revelatory intent of creation (God's sovereign act) and the metaphysical claim that being itself is a continuum linking creature to Creator. Isaiah 40:25 rules out the latter: “To whom then will you liken Me, or to whom shall I be equal?” says the Holy One. God does not stand on the same scale of being as creatures, related to them by proportion. He is the uncreated Creator; they are creatures of His word. The Creator-creature distinction — the ontological line the Reformed tradition draws from the doctrine of God's absolute aseity — means that natural reason cannot ascend from creaturely being to divine Being by analogy of proportion. What creation reveals about God is true, but it is revelation God has given (theologia revelata), not an inference the creature extracts from a shared metaphysical continuum.

Webster 1828 Definition

ANALOGIA ENTIS: Latin, “analogy of being”; the Catholic Thomistic principle that created being stands in proportionate likeness to divine Being, allowing natural reason to ascend from creatures to God; the Reformed tradition accepts general revelation but rejects the metaphysical continuum, grounding all true knowledge of God in God's own revelatory act rather than in a shared scale of being.

ANALOGIA ENTIS. Latin. Analogy of being. The metaphysical principle, formally developed by Thomas Aquinas, that every creature participates in being by a proportionate likeness to the divine Being who is Being Itself (ipsum esse subsistens). On this basis, creaturely terms like “good,” “wise,” and “powerful” can be predicated of God analogically rather than univocally (exactly the same) or equivocally (entirely different).

The Catholic Thomistic tradition treats the analogia entis as the metaphysical foundation for natural theology: the mind can ascend through the Five Ways (Aquinas, Summa Theologica Ia, Q.2, Art.3) from effects to God as their first cause, from motion to the Unmoved Mover, from contingent existence to necessary existence, by virtue of the analogical relationship between created being and divine Being.

Karl Barth (1932, Church Dogmatics I/1) rejected the analogia entis as “the invention of antichrist” and substituted the analogia fidei (analogy of faith): any true knowledge of God comes from God's own self-revelation in Christ, not from a natural metaphysical ascent. Barth's rejection was polemically sharp, but the Reformed tradition's concern is similar: the analogia entis risks treating God and creatures as species of a common genus called “being.”

The Reformed affirmation: general revelation is real and leaves all men without excuse (Rom 1:20). The Reformed qualification: general revelation is God's sovereign act of disclosure, not a metaphysical continuum that the creature's unaided reason may traverse. The Creator-creature distinction is absolute; the analogical knowledge of God given in Scripture (analogia fidei) differs in kind from the Thomistic natural ascent.

Key Scripture

Isa 40:25 — "“To whom then will you liken Me, or to whom shall I be equal?” says the Holy One."

Rom 1:20 — "For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes — His eternal power and divine nature — have been clearly seen, being understood through what has been made. So they are without excuse."

Job 38:4 — "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding."

1 Tim 6:16 — "who alone has immortality — dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or can see. To Him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen."

Modern Corruption

The analogia entis dissolves the Creator-creature distinction by placing God and creatures on a proportionate scale of being, opening the door to natural theology that competes with Scripture as a source of God-knowledge; where it controls interpretation, Christ becomes merely the fullest expression of a being already partially known by reason.

Thomas Aquinas's development of the analogia entis produced the classic Catholic synthesis of Athens and Jerusalem: Aristotelian metaphysics provided the ontological framework within which revealed theology found its place. God is Being Itself (ipsum esse subsistens); creatures share in being by participation; the proportionate likeness between creaturely being and divine Being allows natural theology's ascent from creation to Creator. The practical result in Catholic systematics is that natural reason establishes a prolegomenon to revelation: the existence of God, His unity, His necessary existence, even some attributes, can be known before Scripture speaks. Revelation then supplements what reason already knows. The Reformed tradition rejects the framework: not because the creation is silent about God (it is not; Rom 1:20 insists it speaks clearly) but because the metaphysical claim places God and creatures on a shared scale of being, which the doctrine of divine aseity and simplicity excludes. God does not have being; He is Being. No proportion links creaturely being to divine Being; the Creator-creature distinction is absolute, not graduated.

The deeper theological cost of the analogia entis appears in Christology. If God is already partially known through the natural ascent of reason, then the incarnation becomes the fullest disclosure of what reason was already reaching toward. Christ reveals God more clearly but not in a different register from creation's testimony. The Reformation's insistence is starker: apart from special revelation in Christ and Scripture, the natural mind knows God only in the suppressed and distorted mode of Romans 1:21–23 — knowing the truth and holding it down in unrighteousness. Christ is not a quantitative intensification of natural theology but the qualitative ground of all true knowledge of God. Barth's “invention of antichrist” epithet was polemically excessive, but the concern is genuinely Reformed: wherever the analogia entis controls, Christ tends to shrink.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin analogia (proportion, correspondence) + entis (of being); formally developed by Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) on Aristotelian foundations; the governing principle of Catholic natural theology; contrasted by Barth (1932) and by Reformed theology with the analogia fidei (analogy of faith), which grounds all true God-knowledge in divine revelation.

expand to see more

Aristotle (384–322 BC) — doctrine of analogy in the Categories and Metaphysics: terms are said analogically when they apply to things that share a proportionate relationship rather than an identical nature; Aquinas imported this logical tool into theology to account for how creaturely language can speak truly of a God who transcends creaturely categories

Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), Summa Theologica Ia, QQ.13–14 — formal development of the analogia entis in Christian theology: neither univocal (God's wisdom = human wisdom in the same sense) nor equivocal (entirely different) but analogical (proportionate likeness across the Creator-creature divide)

Latin ens, entis — a being, that which is; from the present participle of esse (to be); in Scholastic metaphysics, being is the most universal transcendental predicated of everything that exists; the analogia entis asks whether God and creatures share this transcendental in a proportionate sense

Karl Barth (1932), Church Dogmatics I/1, preface — the sharpest modern Protestant challenge: “I regard the analogia entis as the invention of antichrist and think that because of it one cannot become Catholic”; Barth's analogia fidei (analogy of faith) substitutes revelation for the natural metaphysical ascent

Herman Bavinck (1854–1921), Reformed Dogmatics — the Reformed orthodox alternative: affirms general revelation and analogical language of God while grounding both in God's sovereign act of self-disclosure rather than in a shared metaphysical continuum; the creature knows God because God speaks, not because being forms a graduated scale linking Creator to creature

Usage

"Reformed apologetics must distinguish clearly between two claims that are easy to conflate: (1) creation reveals God truly (affirmed — Rom 1:20 is clear); (2) creation reveals God by virtue of a metaphysical continuum of being linking creature to Creator (denied — the Creator-creature distinction is absolute). The apologist who accepts claim 1 while rejecting claim 2 can affirm the reality of general revelation without conceding the Thomistic natural-theology project."

"In pastoral ministry, the analogia entis matters because it shapes how people think God can be known. If God is known by an analogy of being, then the mystic who “ascends” through meditation and spiritual discipline toward a direct apprehension of Being Itself is on a continuous path with the theologian. The Reformed tradition insists that God is known as the God who speaks — in creation, in Scripture, supremely in Christ. There is no ascent from being to Being; there is only the condescension of the God who comes down and addresses the creature in human language and in a human person."

"The analogia entis vs. analogia fidei debate has direct implications for ecumenical dialogue with Rome. The Catholic framework assumes a shared natural-theology foundation; the Reformed framework insists that all agreed knowledge of God is knowledge given by God's own revelation and received by faith, not the common fruit of a metaphysical ascent both traditions make. The Protestant-Catholic disagreement is not only about soteriology (justification) but about epistemology: how is God known, and on what basis?"
